title: OExVT-D2CN: One-Shot Enabled External Vision Triplet Attention-Based Distributed Deep Learning Model for Image Recognition
abstract: Evaluation of one-shot-based image recognition contributes to deploying a single input to train a deep learning model regarding the visual concepts. Over the past decades, many researchers have expanded their research on one-shot learning-based image recognition, but failed to achieve accurate performance due to overfitting, insufficient samples, and poor interpretation. Most of the existing approaches cannot provide accurate results when adopts blur images as training samples, which limits efficiency and performance improvements over image recognition experiments. To alleviate such consequences, this research proposes a one-shot-enabled external vision triplet attention-based distributed deep convolutional neural network (OExVT-D2CN) model for effective image recognition. On top of that, this research presents an ExVT module to pay attention to a specific region of the input to enhance recognition stability as well as interpretability. The OExVT-D2CN model accelerates training efficiency by optimizing the input and attenuating challenges on complex datasets and overfitting issues. Based on these hybrid implementation techniques, the proposed model precisely recognizes the objects with minimal computation cost and memory constraints. Furthermore, the OExVT-D2CN model acquires significant results under a one-shot condition, which attains a maximum of 99.41% accuracy and 96.92% precision using the PASCAL VOC-2012 dataset when compared to other state-of-the-art methods.

title: DUMIR: Dynamic Uncertainty-Aware Multimodal Intent Recognition
abstract: Multimodal Intent Recognition (MIR) aims to infer user intentions from textual, acoustic, and visual signals. Existing methods, however, often rely heavily on textual modality while overlooking the dynamic reliability variations of non-text modalities, leading to suboptimal multimodal fusion. To address this issue, we propose a Dynamic Uncertainty-aware Multimodal Intent Recognition framework (DUMIR). Specifically, we estimate modality reliability from the statistical characteristics of multimodal feature sequences and dynamically adjust modality contributions according to their reliability prior to fusion. This strategy effectively reduces the influence of less reliable modality representations and improves fusion robustness. We further design a hierarchical cross-modal interaction architecture to progressively integrate complementary information while preserving modality-specific semantics. In addition, a multi-task joint optimization objective combining fusion supervision, unimodal auxiliary learning, and cross-modal semantic consistency constraints is introduced to enhance representation discriminability and semantic coherence. Experimental results on the MIntRec and MIntRec2.0 benchmarks demonstrate that DUMIR consistently outperforms representative baseline methods across multiple evaluation metrics, achieving accuracies of 76.01% and 61.27%, respectively. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/gongweiyin/DUMIR .

title: ArabXlur: An Arabic Taboo-Language Corpus for Detecting Obfuscated Sexual-Taboo Language (v1.0)
abstract: ArabXlur is a manually annotated corpus of 30,150 Arabic tweets built to study the detection of sexually taboo language that has been orthographically camouflaged to evade automated moderation. In Arabic, dots and diacritics carry phonemic weight and therefore double as instruments of visual disguise (for example, swapping a dotted letter for its dotless placeholder, or padding a word with diacritics). The corpus treats such disguise as a labeled class in its own right. The dataset is balanced across three classes: clean text (label 0), overt taboo in canonical spelling (label 1), and orthographically camouflaged taboo (label 2), 10,050 tweets each. It is released with an 80/20 stratified train/test split (train 24,120; test 6,030) and a 126-item seed lexicon in canonical and disguised forms. Full documentation is in the included README. title: Scaling Intermediate Dataset Size for XLM-R Zero-Shot Transfer Performance on XTREME-R Benchmarks
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: Does scaling the size of the intermediate dataset during English intermediate-task training improve zero-shot transfer performance on XTREME-R benchmarks for XLM-R? Autonomous synthesis report generated by Assignee Research. Tribunal consensus score: 9.3/10.

title: Entropy Regularization in Deep Reinforcement Learning: A Structured Review Across Classical Control, Generative Policies, and Reasoning Language Models
abstract: Entropy regularization is a recurring mechanism in reinforcement learning (RL), but its meaning changes across algorithmic settings. In classical online RL, entropy encourages exploration and smooths policy improvement; in inverse RL and imitation learning, maximum-entropy resolves ambiguity among expert-consistent behaviors; in offline RL, entropy must be balanced against data support; in generative policies, entropy becomes a tractability problem; and in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for large language models (LLMs), token entropy is tied to reasoning diversity, calibration, and collapse. This review organizes these developments into a unified taxonomy. We first summarize the mathematical foundations of maximum-entropy RL, soft Bellman equations, policy-gradient entropy dynamics, and Kullback-Leibler (KL)-constrained mirror descent. We then review entropy in imitation learning, offline RL, intrinsic motivation, diffusion and flow-based policy classes, and RLVR. Particular attention is given to recent work on entropy collapse in reasoning LLMs, entropy-based advantage shaping, covariance-based control, positive-advantage reweighting, and ordinary differential equation (ODE)-based flow-matching policies with tractable entropy. The review emphasizes that entropy is not universally beneficial: useful exploration, support preservation, multimodality, calibration, and reasoning diversity require different entropy objects and different control mechanisms.

title: A survey of inevitability results in AI instability
abstract: Over the past decade, there has been an explosion of activity in the design of algorithms for adversarially attacking artificial intelligence (AI) systems; especially in the context of image classification. For example, a carefully crafted perturbation to an image that is imperceptible to the human eye may cause a sophisticated convolutional neural network to change its classification. To deal with this vulnerability, algorithms that detect or defend against such attacks have also been proposed. It has been observed empirically that attackers have the upper hand. To explain these observations, various theoretical results have subsequently emerged. This article will review some recent rigorous results, emphasizing what assumptions they use, in terms of (i) the nature of the training data, (ii) the network architectures, and (iii) the information available to the attacker. We also discuss how the results may give guidelines for building more secure systems, and how this research area can inform the design of AI regulations. This article is part of the theme issue 'Safe, secure and robust AI for safety-critical systems'.

title: A Dynamic Radial Membrane Architecture
abstract: The U.F.O. (User‑Formed Optimization) research collection introduces a multi‑component systems architecture for adaptive AI behavior, centered on the radial identity membrane—a geometric, compute‑aware representation of AI identity designed to unify personalization, behavioral control, and resource governance. Across the collection, AI behavior is modeled not as a static personality layer but as a dynamical system shaped by user interaction, task pressure, stability constraints, and measurable compute signals. The membrane’s twelve behavioral strings encode dimensions such as depth, precision, initiative, tone, and structural rigor; each string carries amplitude, radius, tension, stiffness, and cost parameters that evolve over time. Adjacent strings blend into V‑shaped reasoning channels, enabling coherent, low‑resistance, cost‑aware routing of activation across related behavioral modes. The broader U.F.O. corpus expands this core architecture through several complementary papers: the Bounded Compute Envelope formalizes the system’s stability and cost limits; Holistic Governor defines the runtime control loop and suppression dynamics; Twelve Strings as Computational Facets details the behavioral basis vectors; Letter Depth Encoding (L.D.E.) introduces a symbolic encoding for membrane geometry; Federated Shard Architecture extends the model to distributed identity routing; Governed Deformable Radial Membrane describes curvature, boundary deformation, and short‑horizon traces; V‑Channel Activation and Kernel Regimes formalizes corridor routing and kernel behavior; and Unified Math in U.F.O. provides the shared mathematical backbone linking membrane geometry, routing, cost, tension, stiffness, and stability. A supervisory U.F.O. governor enforces bounded compute behavior through inverse‑cost routing, suppression functions, tension/stiffness regulation, and a Lyapunov‑style energy term. This governor coordinates runtime inference controls—including reasoning depth, retrieval budget, tool‑call thresholds, tone, and response length—while ensuring compliance with safety, privacy, and policy constraints. Adaptation is framed as data flow across the membrane: inputs excite the interior identity field, propagate through channel‑aligned corridors, and gradually reshape behavioral parameters through reversible, inspectable updates. The accompanying Project Rainbow notebook provides a lightweight toy simulation exercising initialization, activation propagation, channel curvature, governor suppression, bounded depth expansion, and ablation comparisons. Preliminary results across the collection demonstrate internal coherence, stable routing, and controlled compute behavior within the simplified model. While not a production implementation, the U.F.O. research suite offers a testable path toward resource‑aware personalization, suggesting that user‑shaped behavioral control and compute optimization can be integrated into a single governed system suitable for future validation at enterprise scale. This work was originally developed as supplemental documentation for my application to Microsoft Research, where it served as a conceptual demonstration of layered AI governance, compute‑aware behavioral modeling, and systems‑engineering reasoning. The Symmetric Ascension Operator, along with the broader U.F.O. architecture papers, was submitted to illustrate my ability to design formal mechanisms, propose inspectable control surfaces, and articulate validation paths relevant to enterprise‑scale AI systems. The material is presented here in its research form for public reference, scholarly discussion, and archival continuity. It is now published openly to support scholarly reference, public discussion, and archival continuity under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (CC BY 4.0). © 2026 Don Michael Feeney Jr.

title: How Physicists Think Computationally
abstract: How Physicists Think ComputationallyObservation, Modelling, Computation and Physical Insight Physics rarely provides perfect measurements, exact predictions, or complete certainty. Real-world observations contain uncertainty, models involve approximation, and many important physical systems resist exact analytical solutions. How Physicists Think Computationally explores how modern physicists use computation to investigate, model, and understand complex physical systems. Through examples spanning data analysis, numerical methods, simulation, and quantum applications, the book emphasizes physical insight as much as numerical calculation. Designed primarily for postgraduate students of physics, it encourages readers to think beyondformulas and view computation as a powerful extension of scientific reasoning. Observation inspires questions; modelling guides exploration. Computation extends investigation; understanding remains the goal.

title: High-rate continuous-variable quantum key distribution coexisting with Tb/s coherent classical transmission in hollow-core fiber
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) can provide secret keys with security rooted in quantum mechanics, but operation alongside high-capacity classical traffic remains limited by the excess-noise budget of weak quantum states in conventional solid-core fiber. Here, we combine ultralow-loss anti-resonant hollow-core fiber with residual-carrier-assisted discrete-modulation continuous-variable QKD (DM-CV-QKD) to address both propagation-induced coexistence noise and low-SNR phase recovery. Over a 24.3-km hollow-core link with 3.3-dB end-to-end loss, a dual-polarization 15-Gbaud DM-CV-QKD channel achieves an average asymptotic secret-key rate (SKR) of 153.22 Mb/s and a finite-size SKR of 149.99 Mb/s, while 39 coherent wavelength-division-multiplexed channels deliver an aggregate data rate of 7.6 Tb/s and a net data rate of 7.2 Tb/s. The system can even sustain a positive SKR under a high classical launch power of up to 15 dBm, without an optical bandpass filter (BPF). Finite-size analysis against collective attacks further yields a projected positive secret-key rate at a 100-km-equivalent condition. These results show that an anti-resonant hollow-core fiber, combined with carrier-assisted phase recovery, can greatly extend the operating regime of shared-fiber quantum-secured coherent links, pointing to a promising approach for integrating high-rate CV-QKD with high-capacity optical networks.

title: Метод адаптивной калибровки физических симуляционных моделей цифрового двойника по потоку телеметрических данных с применением байесовской оптимизации
abstract: Рассматривается задача калибровки физических симуляционных моделей — в первую очередь моделей на основе метода конечных элементов (МКЭ) — по потоку телеметрических данных от датчиков промышленного оборудования в составе цифрового двойника предприятия. Предложен метод адаптивной калибровки ACBM (Adaptive Calibration via Bayesian-surrogate Minimization), в котором задача идентификации параметров физической модели формулируется как задача максимизации функции правдоподобия L(θ) в пространстве калибруемых параметров θ. Для минимизации числа обращений к вычислительно дорогостоящей МКЭ-симуляции используется суррогатная гауссовская процесс-модель GP(μ, k), обученная на доступных наблюдениях L(θ). Выбор следующей точки для вычисления реализуется через функцию приобретения Expected Improvement (EI). Введён критерий автоматической рекалибровки на основе KL-дивергенции между апостериорным распределением параметров в текущий момент и в момент последней калибровки. Численный анализ выполнен для МКЭ-модели теплового нагрева детали промышленного агрегата с тремя калибруемыми параметрами. Предложенный метод обеспечивает RMSE температуры 1,93°C после 87 обращений к МКЭ-симуляции, что на 97,3% лучше МКЭ-модели с номинальными параметрами и на 16% быстрее стандартной байесовской оптимизации по числу обращений к симуляции.

title: Uso da inteligência artificial na gestão ambiental: desafios e oportunidades
abstract: A crescente intensificação das mudanças climáticas, da degradação ambiental e da pressão sobre os recursos naturais tem ampliado a necessidade de soluções tecnológicas capazes de fortalecer os mecanismos de monitoramento, prevenção e gestão ambiental. Nesse contexto, a Inteligência Artificial (IA) destaca-se como ferramenta estratégica para otimizar processos de análise de dados ambientais, previsão de riscos e apoio à tomada de decisões sustentáveis. O presente estudo tem como objetivo analisar as principais aplicações da Inteligência Artificial na gestão ambiental, identificando suas potencialidades, limitações e desafios contemporâneos. Metodologicamente, trata-se de uma pesquisa qualitativa, de natureza exploratória e analítico-descritiva, desenvolvida por meio de revisão sistemática da literatura e análise interpretativa de evidências empíricas secundárias. Os resultados indicam que a IA contribui significativamente para o monitoramento ambiental, gestão de resíduos, controle de desmatamento, previsão climática e otimização do uso de recursos naturais. Entretanto, persistem desafios relacionados à governança de dados, custos tecnológicos, desigualdade de acesso e questões éticas envolvendo transparência algorítmica e sustentabilidade digital. Conclui-se que a Inteligência Artificial possui elevado potencial transformador na gestão ambiental, desde que sua implementação ocorra de forma ética, regulada e alinhada aos princípios do desenvolvimento sustentável.

title: DoubleF: A Fast and Flexible Phase Association and Earthquake Location Method Using Adaptive Sobol Sampling
abstract: Abstract Earthquake catalogs play a vital role in seismological research. Recent advances in deep learning-based phase picking have greatly enhanced the efficiency and completeness of catalog construction. A crucial step in this workflow is phase association, which links detected phases to their corresponding seismic events. We present DoubleF, a fast and flexible phase association and earthquake location method based on adaptive Sobol sampling. We evaluated DoubleF using three datasets: the 2023 MS 6.2 Jishishan earthquake aftershock sequence, the Baihetan reservoir-induced seismicity from 1 to 31 October 2021, and synthetic data. These experiments were designed to assess the accuracy, robustness to noise, and sensitivity to parameter settings. In real-data experiments, DoubleF generally associated the most events and phases and achieved the highest recall among several widely used methods tested, improving recall by approximately 1% to 4% over the next best method. In synthetic experiments, DoubleF achieved nearly 100% event and phase recall, even when 80% of the phases were noise. Through Sobol-based sampling, matrix parallelization, and graphics processing unit acceleration, the algorithm substantially reduces computation time relative to the tested methods by up to several dozen times. Moreover, the insensitivity of the method to parameter settings ensures its broad applicability, from dense networks for monitoring induced seismicity to sparse regional networks, and makes it particularly well suited for real-time monitoring.

title: Quantum Remote Implementation of Hybrid Operations on Hyperstates Using Hyperentangled States
abstract: Quantum remote control, also known as quantum remote implementation of an operator (QRIO), enables the remote manipulation of an arbitrary quantum state by implementing a desired quantum operation at a distant location. Significant progress has recently been made in developing QRIO protocols and their variants. Most existing schemes employ hyperentangled states where entanglement is shared across multiple degrees of freedom (DOFs). However, these protocols typically exploit only one degree of freedom at a time. In this work, we propose a QRIO protocol that simultaneously utilizes the polarization and spatial DOFs of a two-qubit hyperentangled state to remotely implement an arbitrary hybrid operator on an unknown single-photon two-qubit hyperstate. The shared hyperentangled resource is realized using the polarization and spatial modes of photons, while the protocol is constructed using linear optical elements and cross-Kerr nonlinear interactions to facilitate effective photon-photon coupling. Furthermore, the effects of measurement errors arising from finite coherent state distinguishability and coherent state dissipation are analyzed and the corresponding success probability of the protocol is evaluated. The results demonstrate that an appropriate choice of the cross-Kerr phase shift and coherent state amplitude significantly enhances the protocol performance, making the proposed scheme a promising candidate for hybrid quantum communication and distributed quantum information processing.

title: ANONIMIZAÇÃO DE DADOS SENSÍVEIS EM BANCO DE DADOS CORPORATIVOS
abstract: Em ambientes corporativos, o tratamento inadequado de dados sensíveis pode ampliar riscos de exposição, uso indevido e descumprimento da Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados. Diante desse contexto, este artigo analisa técnicas de anonimização e mascaramento de dados aplicadas a um banco de dados fictício, com o objetivo de avaliar sua contribuição para a proteção de informações sensíveis e para a conformidade com a legislação. A pesquisa caracteriza-se como aplicada, com abordagem mista, combinando revisão bibliográfica e testes experimentais em ambiente controlado. Foram consideradas técnicas como supressão, generalização, permutação, adição de ruído e mascaramento, observando seus impactos sobre a privacidade, a utilidade dos dados e o desempenho do processamento. A análise permitiu comparar as características, vantagens e limitações de cada abordagem, evidenciando que a escolha da técnica mais adequada depende do tipo de dado tratado, da finalidade do uso e do nível de proteção exigido. Conclui-se que a anonimização e o mascaramento são estratégias relevantes para reduzir riscos de exposição de dados em ambientes corporativos.

Diante desse contexto, este artigo analisa técnicas de anonimização e mascaramento de dados aplicadas a um banco de dados fictício, com o objetivo de avaliar sua contribuição para a proteção de informações sensíveis e para a conformidade com a legislação. A pesquisa caracteriza-se como aplicada, com abordagem mista, combinando revisão bibliográfica e testes experimentais em ambiente controlado. Foram consideradas técnicas como supressão, generalização, permutação, adição de ruído e mascaramento, observando seus impactos sobre a privacidade, a utilidade dos dados e o desempenho do processamento. A análise permitiu comparar as características, vantagens e limitações de cada abordagem, evidenciando que a escolha da técnica mais adequada depende do tipo de dado tratado, da finalidade do uso e do nível de proteção exigido. Conclui-se que a anonimização e o mascaramento são estratégias relevantes para reduzir riscos de exposição de dados em ambientes corporativos.

title: Impact of Intermediate Task Selection on Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer in XTREME-R
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: How does the choice of intermediate task (e.g., NLI, QA, or sentiment analysis) influence the zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance on XTREME-R when trained on English-only intermediate tasks, measured by task-specific accuracy and generalization across languages? title: Developing Mathematical Models for Interpretability and Safety Verification of AI-Driven Engineering Systems
abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming established as a component of safety-critical engineering systems such as the autonomous transportation systems, energy infrastructure, industrial automation, and structural monitoring. As much as AI models and especially deep neural networks prove to be more accurate in prediction, their black box nature create serious issues when it comes to interpretability and safety guarantees. In safety critical areas explainability is not only a good idea, but a precursor to regulatory compliance, accountability and mitigation of hazards. This paper creates a comprehensive mathematical conceptualization of using interpretability metrics and formal safety verification protocols of AI-based engineering systems. Based on the recent developments in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), mechanistic interpretability, and formal verification theory, we operationalize interpretability as a measurable functional characterization of model structures and safety verification as meet-in-the-middle of reachable state spaces. Our abstraction of causal circuits and verification of time logics constraints using Shapley-based attribution functions make our integrated optimisation model offer explanation fidelity and safety invariants. The framework illustrates how the measures of interpretability can be integrated in the form of the side-constraints in formal verification pipelines, such that the model decision-making can be transparent and safely proven. Findings suggest that the metrics of coupling explanation coupled with reachability analysis can minimize unsafe decision regions and enhance calibration of the trust. The paper adds a mathematically based architecture that can be able to fill in the gap between heuristic XAI methods and serious engineering safety requirements. It is discussed in implications to aerospace, autonomous systems and industrial control environment as well as computational trade-offs and scalability issues. The model suggested creates a direction towards the certifiable AI systems in which interpretability and safety are not set at cross purposes.

title: lorax: Speak for the Trees
abstract: Extracts decision rules from tree- and rule-based models fitted in 'R'. Rules are expressed as logical predicates that identify paths to terminal nodes, making model behavior more transparent and interpretable. Provides conversion methods to 'partykit' party objects for a wide range of model types. The 'partykit' infrastructure is described in Hothorn and Zeileis (2015) <https://jmlr.org/papers/v16/hothorn15a.html>.

title: Hybrid quantum-classical machine learning for industrial multi-anomaly detection via single acoustic sensor
abstract: We developed a novel workflow that leverages Quantum Kernel feature space expressiveness combined with classical dimensionality reduction techniques. This workflow enables detection and visual identification of multiple simultaneous anomalies using acoustic data from a single non-contact sensor. Our newly developed method provides an intuitive interface for operators to identify specific anomalies. By combining conventional Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCC) with principal component analysis (PCA), the newly constructed Quantum Kernel achieves near-perfect classification (F1 = 1.0 under specific conditions: j ≥ 9 features, file-level data splits) of complex multi-source anomalies, significantly outperforming the classical RBF kernel (F1 ≈ 0.75-0.76) and 1D-CNN autoencoder baseline (F1 ≈ 0.60-0.85). The Quantum Kernel's superior representational power enables accurate anomaly detection with minimal training data. Our results demonstrate simulation-based evidence of potential quantum advantage under ideal conditions, where the performance of our method dramatically exceeds that of classical approaches as the number of features increases, pending validation on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. This hybrid quantum-classical machine learning approach demonstrates significant potential for industrial applications, particularly for complex time-series data in data-scarce regimes where classical methods exhibit limited performance.

title: The Energy Society: A Simulation Environment for Studying Agent Cooperation under Survival Pressure
abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments whose incentives can shape their behavior. We introduce The Energy Society, a minimal survival economy for studying how competitive and cooperative incentives affect emergent behavior when inference cost is directly tied to survival: Agents spend energy based on model size when generating tokens, regain energy by completing jobs or receiving donations, and deactivate if their energy reaches zero. We compare competitive and cooperative objectives against a baseline setting and several control variants. Across experiments, larger models consistently consume the most energy and spend more energy than they gain, even in those settings where token cost is not size-dependent. Cooperative incentives substantially alter behavior: agents donate to reactivate others, sometimes at the cost of their own survival, and job allocation changes. Ablations reveal that allowing agents to recommend actions to each other supports coordination and ambitious job selection, while memory helps agents calibrate risk from past outcomes. Agents rarely choose direct sabotage, but show more subtle signs of self-serving behavior in the competitive setting. The Energy Society is a compact testbed for studying the interaction between token costs and group incentives under a survival pressure. Source code is available at https://github.com/LucasBergholdt/EnergySociety

title: On the Carlet's Bivariate APN Construction and Representations of Dobbertin Power Functions
abstract: In this paper we present necessary and sufficient conditions on some families of bivariate and biprojective APN functions. In the first part, we follow the extended methods given by Calderini et al in 2021, and give sufficient and necessary conditions for Carlet's bivariate APN functions. We also give APN-ness conditions for biprojective functions in some special cases. In the second part, we study the representation of the Dobbertin power function following methods given by Budaghyan et al. in 2022 and give new representations for this kind of functions.

title: BIAI — Session 01 Literature Synthesis Brain-Inspired Artificial Intelligence · AIMS Project · v0.1
abstract: Overview This document records the seven papers ingested during Session 01 of the dedicated BIAI (Brain-Inspired Artificial Intelligence) window, opened as part of the AIMS project. Two upload batches were processed: an initial set of six papers spanning architecture, hardware, and predictive coding, followed by a single paper (Mixture of Cognitive Reasoners, split across two files for upload) with the strongest empirical validation of brain-inspired modularity in the batch. This is a literature-synthesis record, not a formal spec. No DEF/PROP/TCV canon has been established yet for the BIAI window; that is deferred pending direction-setting in a later session (see Section 4, Open Items).

title: When Not to Normalize: Covariance Absorption in Variable-Rate Kalman Innovation Detection
abstract: Kalman innovation statistics are widely used to identify observations that are inconsistent with a tracker’s prediction. Under variable-rate reporting, however, the elapsed time between observations creates a two-sided detection problem. After a reporting gap, process-noise covariance grows rapidly. Normalized innovation squared (NIS) retains its nominal false-positive calibration but loses power against a fixed post-gap displacement. A fixed raw-innovation threshold exhibits the mirror-image failure, increasingly flagging nominal predictions as predictive uncertainty grows. Thus neither normalization nor its removal resolves variable-rate detection: elapsed time must be represented explicitly rather than absorbed into a single score. Controlled anomaly injections across six waterways serve as a mechanistic probe. Raw innovation reaches AUC 0.97 on the injected gap construction, while uncapped NIS reaches 0.65. Real-data validation exposes the boundary of that synthetic result. Five evaluated months of HawaiiCoast_GT contain 200 labeled track segments but only 37 anomalous vessel-months after repeated segments are resolved to the label’s natural unit. Month-stratified vessel-level AUCs for NIS, raw innovation, loiter, and a gap-only control range from 0.55 to 0.59 with overlapping uncertainty. No detector wins convincingly. The results show that synthetic kinematic separability does not transfer cleanly to incident-correlated data and that missingness itself is a necessary control. This record contains the author’s preprint. It has not undergone peer review and may differ from a subsequently accepted or published version.

title: Symbolic knowledge injection & extraction for autonomous learning
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) represents one of humanity’s most transformative technological advancements. In recent years, neuro-symbolic (NeSy) AI has emerged as a promising paradigm for building intelligent systems by integrating symbolic and sub-symbolic approaches. By combining structured reasoning with adaptability and scalability, NeSy AI seeks to overcome the limitations of each paradigm, enabling more robust, interpretable, and reliable systems. Within this framework, this thesis focuses on two complementary subfields of NeSy AI: symbolic knowledge injection (SKI) and symbolic knowledge extraction (SKE). SKI allows structured domain knowledge to be incorporated into sub-symbolic models, guiding learning, improving generalization, and enhancing trustworthiness. Conversely, SKE enables the extraction of symbolic, human-understandable knowledge from such models, addressing the opacity of internal representations and supporting interpretability. Together, SKI and SKE form a synergistic loop: injected knowledge influences learning, while extracted knowledge supports inspection, validation, and refinement, fostering explainable and dependable systems. The thesis investigates the challenges and opportunities of NeSy AI with particular emphasis on SKI and SKE in the engineering of intelligent systems. After reviewing background concepts and the state of the art, we identify key challenges in integrating symbolic and sub-symbolic paradigms. We then present original contributions, including methodologies, algorithms, and tools aimed at advancing NeSy systems. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has further reshaped the AI landscape, offering powerful capabilities for natural language understanding and generation. This thesis explores how LLMs can enhance SKI and SKE, enabling hybrid systems that learn and adapt autonomously. We demonstrate how such approaches can address complex real-world challenges while preserving interpretability and ethical alignment. Finally, we discuss how these contributions advance the broader NeSy vision and support the overarching goal of this thesis: enabling intelligent systems capable of fully autonomous learning through the integration of symbolic reasoning, sub-symbolic learning, and LLMs.

title: Why Companies Fail in Their AI Projects: Lessons from the Frontlines
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been hailed as the transformative force of the 21st century, promising to revolutionize industries from healthcare to finance, retail to manufacturing. Organizations worldwide have rushed to integrate AI into their strategies, with global spending on AI systems expected to surpass $300 billion by 2030. Yet despite the excitement and enormous investment, studies reveal a sobering reality: up to 95% of AI projects fail to deliver on their intended objectives, according to a recent study by MIT .

title: Towards Hierarchical Structure Understanding of Newspaper Images
abstract: Understanding newspaper images remains a challenging task due to their complex, nested hierarchical structures and dense, heterogeneous layouts. In this paper, we explore two complementary approaches for newspaper structure understanding. First, we present a modular bottom-up pipeline that combines state-of-the-art open-source models: YOLO for layout detection, LayoutReader for reading order prediction, and a custom algorithm for article segmentation. This approach leverages existing robust components while maintaining flexibility and interpretability. Second, we introduce Tiramisu (Tiered Transformers for Hierarchical Structure Understanding), a novel end-to-end transformer-based architecture that explicitly models document hierarchy through an iterative tiered process. Tiramisu performs section and article separation, block localization, semantic categorization, and reading order prediction using highly parallelized attention mechanisms. Finally, we release Finlam La Liberté, a new dataset designed specifically for evaluating hierarchical information retrieval in historical newspapers. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of both approaches in reconstructing complex newspaper hierarchies, with comparative analysis highlighting their respective strengths for scalable document digitization. The Tiramisu training code, including the synthetic newspaper generator, is available at https://git.litislab.fr/tiramisu/tiramisu-newspaper-articles-extractor.

title: WrAFT: a Modularized Automated Writing Evaluation System for Argumentative Essays
abstract: This study presents WrAFT, a Writing Assessment and Feedback Tool, that delivers both accurate and reliable scores and effective comprehensive feedback to argumentative essays. WrAFT adopts a modular design by dividing automated writing evaluation (AWE) tasks into scoring, surface-level feedback, and deep-level feedback. In building the system, various Large Language Models (LLMs) have been evaluated, including LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-4o, and Claude 3.7, through both direct prompting and supervised fine-tuning approaches. A proprietary dataset of 480 TOEFL Independent Writing essays with official benchmark scores was utilized. Benchmark-based evaluation shows that WrAFT achieves state-of-the-art performance in scoring, with a quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.84 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.44 against official scores on a scale of 0-5. Human evaluation of system-generated feedback also reveals high approval ratings: 96.14 percent for surface-level feedback, 93.03 percent for deep-level macro feedback, and 94.69 percent for deep-level micro feedback. An interactive user interface has been developed for the system and is publicly available and free to use.

title: Freezing the Notebook: An Interventional Invariant of Capability Formation Across Substrates
abstract: An interventional invariant of capability formation, tested across toy physics, purpose-built mini-networks, and pretrained transformers (GPT-2, Pythia, Qwen2.5, OLMo-2). Define an invariant as a triplet (gesture, signature, kill criterion): an intervention performable identically across substrates, a predicted effect, and a pre-registered outcome that would falsify the claim. The candidate tested here: freezing σ, the slow variable a system writes and rereads (its "notebook"), collapses the capability that σ carries — at inference for an installed capability, and, applied during training, it prevents the capability from ever forming. Across seven capability types and one crossing of the implicit↔explicit divide, the invariant was never falsified. Several of the authors' own hypotheses were, and are reported alongside a training-time causality artifact that was discovered, fixed, and is now guarded against automatically. Two doors: a non-technical walk in ten chapters, and a formal paper. Every claim maps to a runnable command with a pinned environment and registered seeds; the core collapse runs on a laptop in minutes. Code is MIT; texts and figures are CC BY 4.0.

title: AI-Based Credit Card Fraud Detection System Using Machine Learning
abstract: The rapid growth of digital banking, online transactions, and the electronic payment of the systems has been significantly increased the use of credit cards, results in the parallel rise in fraudulent activities. Traditional methods of detecting the fraud are often unable to handle large-scale transaction data and evolving fraud patterns efficiently. This paper presents an AI-Based Credit Card Fraud Detection System using Machine Learning to identify suspicious transactions accurately and in the real time. To identify patterns and detect potential fraud, the proposed system analyzes past transaction data containing various transaction-related attributes amount, merchant details, category, time, and customer information. Data preprocessing techniques including K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) imputation are applied to handle missing values, followed by label encoding and Z-score normalization to improve data quality and consistency. Feature engineering is performed to extract meaningful transaction patterns. The processed data is then classified using the XGBoost algorithm, which improves prediction accuracy through sequential learning and optimized decision trees. Experimental evaluation is carried out using a credit card transaction dataset containing legitimate and fraudulent records.

title: DataShield: Uncovering Risky Fine-Tuning Data Across LLMs Through Consensus Subspace Alignment
abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on domain-specific datasets has become a standard paradigm for adapting LLMs to specialized applications. However, recent work has shown that even fine-tuning on benign task-specific data can substantially weaken the safety capabilities of LLMs. While existing efforts have made progress in identifying data responsible for safety degradation, they usually rely on a single mean vector computed over a specific model with its tokenizer to represent the safety direction, which limits both the effectiveness and transferability of their risk assessment measures. To address these limitations, we propose DataShield, a data assessment framework that identifies risky fine-tuning samples and response segments through consensus subspace alignment over joint safety-critical semantic spaces derived from multiple safety-aligned LLMs. Within these spaces, DataShield extracts consensus safe and unsafe subspaces using semantic spectral decomposition over safe and unsafe data representations. The risk of a data sample or segment is then estimated by measuring its relative alignment with the unsafe and safe subspaces, enabling both sample-level filtering and fine-grained segment-level masking. Compared with state-of-the-art filtering and masking baselines, DataShield reduces ASR by 14.6\% with sample filtering and 32.3\% with segment masking, while preserving downstream utility and avoiding target-model-specific risk computation.

title: Generalized Process Simulation of Heterogeneous Industrial Robots Using a Shared Machine Learning Model
abstract: Industrial robot process simulation plays an important role in production planning, optimization, and digital twin development. However, many existing simulation approaches rely on robot-specific and manually parametrized models, which limits scalability in heterogeneous robot environments. This paper proposes a unified machine learning–based simulation framework for modelling and simulating process behaviour across different industrial robot platforms using a shared task-space learning policy. The proposed approach combines reinforcement learning and inverse kinematics with clearly separated roles. The reinforcement learning policy generates end-effector motion in task space, while inverse kinematics converts the desired motion into robot-specific joint configurations and supports geometric feasibility. This separation reduces the dependence of the learning model on the joint structure of a particular robot. Experimental evaluation on heterogeneous robot platforms showed that the proposed framework can learn accurate target-reaching behaviour in simulation. The best-performing policy achieved a success rate close to 1.0, a mean final distance error of 0.0082 m, and a mean final orientation error of 5.55°. These results indicate that a shared task-space learning policy combined with robot-specific inverse kinematics can support scalable robot process simulation.

title: FlowEqProp: Training Flow Matching Models with Gradient Equilibrium Propagation
abstract: We introduce Gradient Equilibrium Propagation (GradEP), a mechanism that extends Equilibrium Propagation (EP) to train energy gradients rather than energy minima, enabling EP to be applied to tasks where the learning objective depends on the velocity field of a convergent dynamical system. Instead of fixing the input during dynamics as in standard EP, GradEP introduces a spring potential that allows all units, including the visible units, to evolve, encoding the learned velocity in the equilibrium displacement. The spring and resulting nudge terms are both purely quadratic, preserving EP’s hardware plausibility for neuromorphic implementation. As a first demonstration, we apply GradEP to flow matching for generative modelling — an approach we call FlowEqProp — training a two-hidden-layer MLP (24,896 parameters) on the Optical Recognition of Handwritten Digits dataset using only local equilibrium measurements and no backpropagation. The model generates recognisable digit samples across all ten classes with stable training dynamics. We further show that the time-independent energy landscape enables extended generation beyond the training horizon, producing sharper samples through additional inference-time computation — a property that maps naturally onto neuromorphic hardware, where longer relaxation yields higher-quality outputs. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of EP training a flow-based generative model.

title: An Introduction to Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics for Engineering Applications
abstract: Many engineering problems involve phenomena whose governing equations are poorly characterized or only partially known. Surrogate modeling techniques such as neural networks can capture the behavior of these systems, but they typically demand large training datasets that are difficult to obtain in engineering contexts and yield models with limited physical interpretability. The Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) method addresses both limitations by performing sparse regression over libraries of candidate nonlinear terms, recovering interpretable governing equations from comparatively small datasets. Although SINDy has been demonstrated extensively on canonical benchmark systems, its application to practical engineering problems is less widely documented. This tutorial introduces the SINDy method and progressively builds toward its main extensions, from noise-robust weak-form and ensembling-based variants to constrained and parametrizable formulations. The paper and the accompanying tutorial (available at https://github.com/paullililili/SINDy4Engineers) is organized in three parts: the first introduces the standard SINDy algorithm and progressively extends it, inviting readers without prior knowledge to follow each step and adapt the methods to their own problems; the remaining two parts present detailed case studies on (1) the system identification of an unmanned aerial vehicle and (2) a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger. Through these examples, we aim to demonstrate that SINDy is simple to implement yet flexible enough to serve as a valuable identification tool for advanced engineering applications.

The paper and the accompanying tutorial (available at https://github.com/paullililili/SINDy4Engineers) is organized in three parts: the first introduces the standard SINDy algorithm and progressively extends it, inviting readers without prior knowledge to follow each step and adapt the methods to their own problems; the remaining two parts present detailed case studies on (1) the system identification of an unmanned aerial vehicle and (2) a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger. Through these examples, we aim to demonstrate that SINDy is simple to implement yet flexible enough to serve as a valuable identification tool for advanced engineering applications.

title: Random Access to LZ-End: Faster and Deterministic
abstract: The LZ-End parsing of a length-$n$ string is a variation of Lempel-Ziv compression introduced by Kreft and Navarro [DCC 2010], motivated by the lack of a linear-size structure with $O(\log n)$ access time for the classical variant. While the original paper was only able to provide efficient extraction from the phrase boundaries, recently Kempa and Saha [SODA 2022] established that, for a string $S$ whose LZ-End parsing consists of $z$ phrases, there exists a random access data structure that uses $O(z)$ space and guarantees $O(\log^{4}n \cdot \log\log n)$ query time. However, their proof does not yield an efficient construction algorithm, and their data structure is inherently randomized. We resolve both limitations by providing a deterministic, $O(z)$-space data structure that supports random access queries in polylogarithmic time and can be constructed in $O(z\log^{2}(n/z))$ time directly from the LZ-End parsing. In addition to eliminating randomness and providing an efficient construction algorithm, the query time of our data structure is $O(\log^{2}(n/z))$, significantly improving upon the query time of Kempa and Saha. We also show that our techniques can be used to support the more general substring-extraction. Namely, we present a data structure with the same space and the same construction time that given two indices $i$ and $j$, outputs $S[i..j]$ in $O(j-i+\log^2\frac{n}{z})$ time.

title: Democratizing Agent Deployment Safety: A Structural Monitoring Approach
abstract: AI software development agents are increasingly capable of modifying infrastructure and security critical systems, creating risks where an agent completes its assigned task while covertly weakening safeguards through actions such as broadening permissions, degrading logging, or introducing persistence mechanisms. While frontier laboratories may deploy sophisticated monitoring pipelines, many organizations and individual users adopting coding agents lack the resources and governance maturity required to maintain complex learned monitor ensembles. We study this problem as infrastructure level sabotage under task success in the infrastructure-as-code setting from ControlArena and compare trained and untrained monitors across synchronous and asynchronous deployment modes. We introduce an Information Flow Graph (IFG) monitor that analyzes structural security regressions using control-flow and data-flow graph diffs alongside raw code diffs. In asynchronous evaluation, an untrained git diff monitor misses 11.6% attacks at 1% false positive rate auditing budget, our untrained IFG monitor reduces this to 3.5%, and the trained Async RF monitor achieves below 1%. Unlike the trained Async RF monitor, IFG can also operate synchronously as a pre-deployment safeguard that blocks suspicious infrastructure changes before execution or merge. In synchronous mode, IFG realtime rollback reduces joint main task and covert task success from 74.4% to 0.0% with no measurable reduction in legitimate task completion. These results suggest that untrained structural monitors provide a practical and auditable path toward democratizing deployment safety for organizations seeking trustworthy adoption of advanced AI agents.

title: TADG-RAG Replication Package: TADG-Bench, Code, Model Outputs, and Evaluation Results
abstract: This record contains the complete versioned replication package for the study “TADG-RAG: Governing-Claim Resolution for Defensible Enterprise Decisions under Temporal, Authority, and Scope Constraints.” The package includes the frozen corpus of 305 traceable atomic claims, TADG-Bench with 120 independently reviewed cybersecurity policy scenarios, source acquisition and provenance records, annotation codebooks, validation and re-audit materials, retrieval baselines, structured Claude Sonnet 5 and Qwen3-32B outputs, the metadata-aware resolver implementation, fold assignments, overlap audits, robustness experiments, grouped holdout evaluations, figures, tables, manifests, and cryptographic checksums. The package supports auditability and reproduction of the principal results reported in the manuscript. Limitations of the retained Qwen3-32B execution environment are explicitly documented, and unavailable settings have not been reconstructed post hoc.

title: **Model Size and Intermediate-Task Training for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer on XTREME Benchmarks**
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: What is the impact of model size (e.g., 1B vs. 7B vs. 13B parameters) on the effectiveness of English intermediate-task training for zero-shot cross-lingual transfer on XTREME benchmarks? Autonomous synthesis report generated by Assignee Research. Tribunal consensus score: 8.5/10.

title: AOI v4 Piggyback LLM Reference Library — 24-Model Survey (Closed API + Open-Weight), Confirming the LLM-Free Confidence Gate
abstract: Reference survey only. AOI v4's confidence gate resolves abstentions without calling any of these models; no API/token spend occurs in the current pipeline. See related identifier for the AOI v4 engine itself (10.5281/zenodo.21368154). Reference docs for 24 LLMs, organized as an optional "piggyback" resource for AOI v4 — none of these are runtime dependencies of AOI v4, which remains numpy-only and needs no LLM to run. This library exists so AOI v4's confidence-gate abstentions have somewhere to optionally escalate to later, and so open-weight models can be pulled locally on demand. Compiled from public provider documentation (pricing pages, model cards, official docs) — this is a documentation survey, not original research or a novelty claim. Closed / API-only (no local weights possible): Claude Fable 5, Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Opus 4.8 (Anthropic); Gemini (Google); Grok (xAI). Open-weight (downloadable from Hugging Face): Qwen (Alibaba), Llama (Meta), Mistral (Mistral AI), DeepSeek, Gemma (Google), Phi (Microsoft), Falcon (TII), Yi (01.AI), Command-R (Cohere), StableLM (Stability AI, inactive since Apr 2024), MPT (MosaicML/Databricks, superseded by DBRX), BLOOM (BigScience), Pythia (EleutherAI), OLMo (Allen Institute for AI), Jamba (AI21 Labs), GLM (Zhipu AI/Z.ai), Baichuan, InternLM (Shanghai AI Lab), Aya (Cohere For AI). Each card documents provider, license, context window, capabilities, and (where applicable) API pricing, plus a note on how that model could optionally plug into AOI v4's confidence gate as an escalation layer for abstained cases — strictly hypothetical, never a dependency. Licensing varies widely across the open-weight set: Apache 2.0/MIT (Qwen, DeepSeek, Phi, Yi, GLM, InternLM, OLMo — cleanest for commercial use) vs. non-commercial or usage-gated (Command-R, Aya Expanse/Vision, Jamba 1.5+, Falcon).

title: An intelligence-based approach to lung CT image classification: A PSO-optimized deep learning framework for slice-level malignancy detection
abstract: Background and objective Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, making early and precise evaluation via computed tomography (CT) imaging essential. While artificial intelligence offers promising analytical aids, mitigating overfitting on restricted medical datasets and selecting optimally efficient architectures remain persistent challenges. This study proposes an intelligence-based framework integrating Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) to enhance automated slice-level binary classification (malignant versus normal/benign). Methods We systematically evaluated five distinct CNN architectures (VGG16, VGG19, ResNet-50, InceptionV3, and a Modified LeNet) using a unified dataset comprising 3 , 197 scans from the IQ-OTH/NCCD and LIDC-IDRI cohorts. To systematically mitigate data leakage, strict patient-level data partitioning (integrated with a nested cross-validation framework) was implemented. A metaheuristic PSO algorithm was utilized to autonomously optimize critical model hyperparameters—specifically learning rate, batch size, and weight decay—tailoring the networks to effectively process two-dimensional CT slices. Results Empirical findings demonstrated that deeper architectures are highly susceptible to overfitting and feature redundancy in this specific context, with VGG19 and InceptionV3 yielding overall accuracies of 67.46 % and 86.72 % , respectively. In contrast, the PSO-optimized Modified LeNet achieved superior performance for slice-level classification, yielding an overall test accuracy of 97.27 % , alongside a sensitivity of 96.08 % and a specificity of 98.47 % . Conclusions Contrary to the prevailing assumption that deeper networks universally provide superior performance, this study establishes that a lightweight, PSO-tuned architecture is highly effective and computationally efficient for slice-level binary medical imaging classification. By circumventing overfitting and reducing computational overhead, this meticulously optimized framework demonstrates significant potential as a robust computational aid for radiological evaluation.

title: ARMOR++: Agentic Orchestration of a Multi-Domain Primitive Set for Transferable Attacks on Deepfake Detectors
abstract: The reliability of deepfake detectors frequently degrades under black-box adversarial transfer, as these models often rely on fragile, architecture-dependent forensic cues. Existing transfer attacks often lack semantic awareness and struggle to maintain effectiveness under strict no-query constraints, particularly when perturbations are transferred from convolutional surrogates to transformer-based targets. To address these limitations, this paper introduces ARMOR++, a robust multi-agent framework designed for high-transferability deepfake evasion. The framework leverages the Qwen2.5-VL Vision-Language Model (VLM) to supply spatial semantic priors, while the Qwen3 Large Language Model (LLM) orchestrates primitive selection, adaptive hyperparameter reparameterization, and entropy-regularized perturbation mixing. By integrating five complementary primitives, spanning dense optimization, saliency-based methods, spatial transformations, frequency-domain perturbations, and block-structured modifications, ARMOR++ effectively targets heterogeneous inductive biases. Rigorous evaluation on the AADD-2025 benchmark demonstrates that ARMOR++ significantly outperforms existing agentic and non-agentic baselines across both low- and high-quality image regimes. Statistical analysis confirms a substantial gain in blind-target Attack Success Rate (ASR) over the state-of-the-art agentic baseline, with further performance advantages evidenced against non-agentic benchmarks and under robust defensive configurations. These findings highlight a significant residual reliability gap in current deepfake detector deployments and demonstrate the efficacy of agentic orchestration in identifying latent vulnerabilities.

title: Statistics of the Compression Ratio of a Variable-to-Variable Code: Exact Moments and Asymptotic Behavior
abstract: A variable-to-variable (V2V) length code parses a source sequence into phrases of variable length and maps each phrase to a binary codeword of, generally, a different random length. After encoding $n$ phrases, the realized compression ratio $R_n=Λ_n/Σ_n$ -- total codeword length over total source-symbol count -- is the finite-sample counterpart of the code's asymptotic rate $ρ$, to which it converges only as $n\to\infty$. This paper first derives exact formulas for all integer moments of $R_n$ for a given discrete memoryless source (DMS). Specifically, we obtain a closed-form formula for every moment $\E\{R_n^k\}$ as a one-dimensional integral involving only single-phrase moment generating functions of the pair $(L,\ell)$ -- the phrase length, in source symbols, and codeword length, in bits. From these moments we derive an Edgeworth approximation to the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of $R_n$ that is substantially more accurate than the central limit theorem (CLT) approximation. Using the Laplace method of integration, we also derive explicit closed-form formulas for the bias constant $C=\lim_{n\to\infty}n(\E\{R_n\}-ρ)$ and for the variance constant $\lim_{n\to\infty}n\cdot\Var\{R_n\}$. The analysis extends to Markov sources via state-indexed matrices with a redundancy formula obtained in closed form. On the coding-theoretic side, we cast V2V length codes as finite-state encoders and apply a generalized Kraft inequality for a compression-rate lower bound, and give a structural decomposition of the bias coefficient that separates cleanly across variable-to-fixed (V2F) length codes, fixed-to-variable (F2V) length codes, and V2V length codes. Applied to the Khodak code of Bugeaud, Drmota, and Szpankowski, this decomposition shows that its improved performance is reflected in its smaller bias constant.

title: ІНЖЕНЕРІЯ ПРОГРАМНИХ СИСТЕМ СМАРТРЕГІОНУ Фінансові сервіси, кіберстійкість і реінжиніринг бізнес-процесів
abstract: Колективна монографія присвячена теоретико- методологічним і прикладним засадам інженерії програмних систем смартрегіону, що забезпечують функціонування фінансових сервісів, кіберстійкість та адаптивний реінжиніринг бізнес-процесів. Фінансова установа розглядається як постачальник критичних програмно реалізованих сервісів у взаємозалежній регіональній екосистемі. У виданні інтегровано три напрями: інженерію інтелектуальних програмних систем і даних; кібербезпеку та операційну стійкість; реінжиніринг процесів і керування реалізацією економічних вигод. Запропоновані моделі поєднують інженерію вимог, архітектуру програмного забезпечення, інженерію даних, штучний інтелект, process mining, Zero Trust, DevSecOps, MLOps, безперервність діяльності та оцінювання TCO/ROSI. Програмні рішення трактуються не як самодостатня технологічна мета, а як керовані системи з вимірюваними характеристиками якості, вартості, ризику, продуктивності та стійкості. Розрахункові приклади мають статус авторської апробації на знеособленому синтетичному профілі й потребують локального калібрування. title: Formal Lean Verification of the Structural Collatz Infinite Tree (Natural Mathematics)
abstract: Abstract This document presents the complete Lean formalization supporting the structural proof of Collatz termination within Natural Mathematics. Lean formally verifies the following structural statement: “The Collatz inverse graph forms a rooted infinite tree with unique parent, unique root, and no cycles.” This structural statement is mathematically equivalent to the standard Collatz conjecture: “Every natural number reaches 1 in finitely many Collatz steps.” Lean does not formalize numerical termination directly. Instead, it proves the structural conditions that force termination, thereby closing the Collatz infinite tree as a formal mathematical object.

title: Effectiveness of Intermediate-Task Training on Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Performance in XTREME-R Across Model Sizes
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: Does the effectiveness of English intermediate-task training on zero-shot cross-lingual performance in XTREME-R vary when comparing smaller (e.g., 110M parameters) versus larger (e.g., 7B+ parameters) pretrained models? title: Can AI Build a Time Machine? Exploring the Science, Limits, and Speculative Future of Time Travel
abstract: The idea of time travel has captivated human imagination for centuries, from H.G. Wells’ The Time Machine to blockbuster films like Interstellar and Back to the Future . At its core, time travel challenges our very understanding of existence, causality, and reality. As artificial intelligence (AI) rapidly advances, transforming industries and enabling machines to solve complex problems, the question arises: Can AI help us build a time machine? This article explores that question by examining the science of time travel, the capabilities and limitations of AI, and whether their convergence might one day unlock the secrets of temporal movement.

title: SUFLECA: Scaling Up Feature Learning for CAD-to-image Alignment
abstract: CAD-to-image alignment aims to estimate an object's 9D pose (rotation, translation, and anisotropic scale) from a single RGB image, enabling applications in robotics and augmented reality. Recent zero-shot methods use visual foundation models to match image regions to CAD models, yet typically their correspondences are appearance-driven and degrade under occlusion or sim-to-real domain shift. To address these limitations, we introduce SUFLECA (Scaling Up Feature LEarning for CAD Alignment), a weakly-supervised framework for zero-shot CAD alignment with two key contributions. First, SUFLECA scales up geometry-grounded feature learning from pretrained visual representations through Normalized Object Coordinates (NOCs) supervision on 674K images spanning 12 real and synthetic datasets, learning compact geometry-aware features that generalize across domains. Second, we propose a geometrically consistent matching algorithm that establishes reliable one-to-one CAD-to-image correspondences. Together, these contributions enable accurate, sub-second alignment per object instance without iterative pose refinement. On ScanNet25k, SUFLECA achieves 33.4%/42.3% category/instance accuracy, outperforming, with a smaller computational footprint, the strongest zero-shot baseline by 10.3/12.2 percentage points and, for the first time on this benchmark, even surpassing fully supervised methods. Code is available at: https://github.com/snt-arg/SUFLECA

title: Probabilistic "Copies" in Generative AI Models
abstract: Recent work shows that it is possible to extract verbatim or near-verbatim text of some copyrighted works from some large language models (LLMs or models). That is evidence that the model weights encode the works in some form - that the model has "memorized" those works from its training data. But LLMs don't store information in the same format as familiar databases. Rather, their weights store statistical relationships between tokens that have been learned from the training data, and those relationships inform a generation process that is often probabilistic rather than deterministic. In the case of memorization, those relationships are strong enough that, in many circumstances, the model might generate a copyrighted work from its training data with some probability. Copyright law has not previously had to decide whether storing information that might or might not produce output similar to a copyrighted work is itself a copy of the work. The answer to the question is important, because it may determine the legality of many LLMs. The statute and case law are largely unhelpful. We argue that copyright law will likely take a functional approach to the question, finding that LLMs contain a copy of a particular work only if it is straightforward to extract that work in outputs. That result is unsatisfying as a policy matter, and we suggest potential changes to the law, but it is the most likely outcome under current law.

title: Apple, Siri, and the DMA: Execution-Finality as the Missing Layer in Every Compliance Proposal So Far
abstract: When "Interoperability" and "Security" Can't Both Be True Every major platform now faces the same unsolved technical contradiction: regulators require that third-party AI assistants receive execution access equivalent to a platform's own first-party assistant. Platform operators require that this access never translates into uncontrolled authority over irreversible device actions — payments, message sends, file exports, credential release, sensor capture. Every attempted fix so far has lived entirely in software: permission dialogs, entitlement frameworks, OAuth scopes, developer policy agreements. Software-layer solutions fail for a structural reason — the same layer that grants access also controls how that access is described, audited, and revoked. A vendor policing itself cannot independently prove it granted genuine parity to a competitor. The problem, precisely stated: no existing architecture separates the request for a device action from the authority to actually perform it, at the hardware level, for every assistant equally. The solution: treat every device-side action — regardless of which app, assistant, or AI agent requests it — as a Candidate Act held in a non-effective state. Before it can do anything, a hardware-isolated execution domain (Secure Enclave, ARM TrustZone, Android StrongBox, Titan M) independently validates a fixed set of predicates: application identity, declared purpose, resource scope, destination, runtime behavior, and freshness. Only if every predicate is satisfied does the domain release a scoped, single-use, non-transferable capability — bound to that one act and nothing else. The operating system stays in the loop as a mediator: it can route requests, gather evidence, and carry the capability object — but it cannot mint, expand, reinterpret, or force acceptance of that capability. Final authority sits entirely outside its reach. At the exact boundary where the action would take effect, a Finality Sink checks the capability one more time. If anything has changed — identity, scope, destination, freshness — the action is refused. No partial execution. No fallback path. Fail closed, always. Why this closes the deadlock: first-party and third-party assistants are evaluated under identical predicates, enforced by hardware rather than platform policy — giving regulators verifiable parity they don't have to take on trust. Platform operators get a guarantee that no assistant, including their own, can ever obtain uncontrolled execution authority — because requesting, approving, and previewing an action is never the same thing as making it happen.

title: Banya AI 5: Cache-Dictionary Tokenization and Dynamic Embedding , Near-Free Vocabulary Expansion via a Low-Rank Head
abstract: Tokenization - splitting text into the word units a model handles - is arranged in two layers. The lower layer consists of syllable atoms (Korean phonetic units), and the upper layer is a bundle dictionary that holds frequent words as whole tokens. The vocabulary of the measured model stacks 8000 bundles on top of 2724 syllable atoms, for a total of 10724. Ordinarily, increasing the vocabulary fourfold makes the output head (the final layer that selects the next word) proportionally more expensive in parameters, but this paper makes vocabulary expansion nearly free by giving the output head a low-rank form (approximating the large matrix as a product of two smaller matrices). At vocabulary 10724, channel width 1024, and rank 128, the low-rank head has about 1.5 million parameters, about 7.3 times fewer than the dense head's about 10.98 million. Furthermore, bundle-layer tokens preserve the orthogonal structure of the data plane and the operation plane intact (the operator emergence of Part 3 also appears in bundles, with a direction consistency of 8.1 times). That is, the cache dictionary gains compression without breaking the data-operation structure established by the earlier papers. We also measured that the savings travel together with quality. The normal path, bundles on, predicts holdout text at 5.08 bits per character while encoding the same text with 21.5% fewer tokens; with bundles off, prediction collapses at word-internal positions (11.49 bits per token vs. 6.69 at boundaries), revealing that this system's word knowledge resides in the bundle path. This record contains the English edition (_en.pdf) and the Korean original (_kr.pdf). Part 5 of the six-part Banya AI research series. Part 1: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21385447. Part 2: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21385516. Part 3: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21385676. Part 4: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21385699. All measured figures are reproducible with the public code package: https://ubmscoin.github.io/banya/banya_ai_paper_code/ (code Apache-2.0). Frozen model checkpoints: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21383724

title: Αξιολόγηση Τεχνικών Συμπίεσης για Μεγάλα Γλωσσικά Μοντέλα
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly in recent years, fundamentally transforming the field of Artificial Intelligence.Due to their impressive ability to understand and generate natural language, they have become invaluable tools across a wide range of applications.However, these abilities are only realizable on hardware that is able to meet their demanding computational and operational requirements.The scale of modern models, which spans billions of parameters, requires massive memory resources and processing power.Consequently, serving these models becomes exceptionally expensive in data centers and prohibitive for executing large and capable models on consumer hardware.To bridge the gap between computational demands and hardware limitations, research has focused on neural network compression techniques, most notably quantization and weight pruning.Quantization aims to reduce the numerical precision of model weights and activations, whereas pruning selectively removes weights to create sparse tensors.Both methods aim to restrict the memory footprint without significantly compromising model quality.This thesis investigates the application, optimization, and evaluation of these compression methodologies by thoroughly examining the trade-offs between model quality and hardware efficiency during execution.The experimental analysis is structured into two distinct stages.The first stage evaluates system performance in terms of throughput, power, and energy consumption across various compressed configurations.This analysis is conducted exclusively utilizing the vLLM framework in order to maintain compatibility and ensure a fair evaluation.The second stage of this work is dedicated entirely to assessing the quality of the compressed models by benchmarking several state-of-the-art quantization and pruning algorithms.Furthermore, beyond a comparative evaluation of existing methodologies, this thesis proposes a specific modification to the HQQ quantization framework, which enhances the final compression quality.Overall, the findings of this work highlight critical design choices for selecting model configurations that meet both quality and hardware constraints.

evidence.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly in recent years, fundamentally transforming the field of Artificial Intelligence.Due to their impressive ability to understand and generate natural language, they have become invaluable tools across a wide range of applications.However, these abilities are only realizable on hardware that is able to meet their demanding computational and operational requirements.The scale of modern models, which spans billions of parameters, requires massive memory resources and processing power.Consequently, serving these models becomes exceptionally expensive in data centers and prohibitive for executing large and capable models on consumer hardware.To bridge the gap between computational demands and hardware limitations, research has focused on neural network compression techniques, most notably quantization and weight pruning.Quantization aims to reduce the numerical precision of model weights and activations, whereas pruning selectively removes weights to create sparse tensors.Both methods aim to restrict the memory footprint without significantly compromising model quality.This thesis investigates the application, optimization, and evaluation of these compression methodologies by thoroughly examining the trade-offs between model quality and hardware efficiency during execution.The experimental analysis is structured into two distinct stages.The first stage evaluates system performance in terms of throughput, power, and energy consumption across various compressed configurations.This analysis is conducted exclusively utilizing the vLLM framework in order to maintain compatibility and ensure a fair evaluation.The second stage of this work is dedicated entirely to assessing the quality of the compressed models by benchmarking several state-of-the-art quantization and pruning algorithms.Furthermore, beyond a comparative evaluation of existing methodologies, this thesis proposes a specific modification to the HQQ quantization framework, which enhances the final compression quality.Overall, the findings of this work highlight critical design choices for selecting model configurations that meet both quality and hardware constraints.
